keyVerseText: And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Manasseh: that is, Forgetting
rootMeaning: The Hebrew name מְנַשֶּׁה (Menashsheh) derives from the root נָשָׁה (nâshâh), which fundamentally means 'to forget' or 'to cause to forget.' This root conveys not only the act of forgetting but also the idea of removing or remitting something. The literal sense of 'causing to forget' adds depth to the name beyond a mere label, implying a divine action of releasing or setting aside past burdens or hardships.
usageInScripture: The word מְנַשֶּׁה appears 146 times in Scripture, primarily as a proper name referring to the eldest son of Joseph and the tribe descending from him. The most frequent translations, such as 'of Manasseh' and 'Manasseh,' highlight its consistent use as a tribal and personal name. This usage underscores the importance of Manasseh as both an individual and a collective identity in biblical history, with occasional references to his territorial and genealogical significance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מְנַשֶּׁה as 'causing to forget' enriches our grasp of God's providence and grace in Scripture. It reflects how God can bring healing and renewal by enabling His people to move beyond past sufferings and failures. The name embodies the hope that God’s intervention can remove the weight of toil and hardship, pointing to the spiritual truth that in Christ, believers are forgiven and set free from the burden of sin and memory of past guilt. This divine forgetfulness is not mere oblivion but a gracious act that restores relationship and hope.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 41:51 states, 'And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.' Here, the name Manasseh explicitly expresses the meaning of 'forgetting' as a divine act. Joseph recognizes that God has caused him to forget his previous hardships, signifying a new beginning and God's faithfulness in turning suffering into blessing. The word מְנַשֶּׁה in this verse captures the profound reality that God’s grace can erase the pain of the past and open the way to restoration.
